title: Production evaluation & monitoring
summary: Measure whether your deployed AI app is actually good, then watch it in production so you catch problems before users do.
objectives: Explain why offline evaluation and live monitoring are both needed
Build a small labelled eval set and run it automatically
Choose sensible metrics: accuracy, latency, cost, and quality
Use an LLM-as-judge to score open-ended outputs
Log every request and response for later inspection
Track latency, error rate, and token cost in production
Set alerts and watch for drift so quality does not silently rot

quiz.q: What is the difference between offline evaluation and production monitoring?
quiz.answer: Offline evaluation runs your system against a fixed test set before deploying; monitoring watches real live traffic after deploying.
quiz.why: Evaluation answers 'is it good enough to ship?'; monitoring answers 'is it still good now that real users are hitting it?'.

quiz.q: Why might you use an LLM as a judge instead of exact string matching?
options: Open-ended answers can be correct in many wordings, so exact match fails
It removes the need for any test set
quiz.why: For free-text outputs there is no single right string, so a judge model can score correctness, relevance, or tone where exact match would wrongly fail valid answers.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a metric you would typically monitor in production?
options: Number of lines of code in the repo
quiz.why: Latency, error rate, and cost are live operational signals; lines of code is a static repo property, not something you watch in production.

quiz.q: What does 'drift' mean in a deployed AI system?
quiz.answer: When real-world inputs or model behaviour gradually change so that quality degrades even though the code has not changed.
quiz.why: User questions evolve and models or data shift over time; drift is why a system that passed evals at launch can quietly get worse later.

quiz.q: Why is p95 latency often more useful than average latency?
options: It shows the experience of your slowest 5% of users, who feel the pain
quiz.why: An average can look fine while a tail of very slow requests ruins the experience for some users; p95 surfaces that tail.

quiz.q: Name one thing you should log for every request to support later debugging.
quiz.answer: The input prompt, the model output, latency, token usage, and a timestamp (any one of these is acceptable).
quiz.why: Structured logs let you reproduce failures, spot regressions, and trace cost and latency back to specific requests.

body_markdown:
## Why evaluation and monitoring matter

You have built an AI feature, wired in the Claude Messages API, and deployed it. But how do you *know* it works — and keeps working? Two practices answer this.

**Offline evaluation** runs your system against a fixed test set *before* you ship. It answers: is this good enough to release?

**Production monitoring** watches real live traffic *after* you ship. It answers: is it still good now that real users are hitting it?

A system can pass every eval at launch and still degrade later as user questions change or the world moves on. You need both.

## Build an eval set

An eval set is a small collection of representative inputs with expected outputs (or grading rules). Even 20–50 hand-picked cases catch a surprising number of regressions. Run them automatically so every change is checked.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

cases = [
    {"input": "What is 2 + 2?", "expected": "4"},
    {"input": "Capital of France?", "expected": "Paris"},
]

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip()

passed = sum(c["expected"] in answer(c["input"]) for c in cases)
print(f"{passed}/{len(cases)} passed")
```

## Pick the right metrics

Different questions need different numbers. Track a handful:

- **Accuracy / quality** — did the answer meet the expected result or rubric?
- **Latency** — how long did it take? Watch **p95**, not just the average, so the slow tail does not hide.
- **Cost** — tokens in plus tokens out, times the price per token.
- **Error rate** — fraction of requests that failed or were refused.

For open-ended answers there is no single correct string, so exact matching fails. Use an **LLM-as-judge**: ask a model to score the output against a rubric.

```python
def judge(question: str, response: str) -> int:
    prompt = (
        f"Question: {question}\n"
        f"Answer: {response}\n"
        "Score the answer 1-5 for correctness. Reply with only the number."
    )
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=8,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return int(msg.content[0].text.strip())
```

## Log and monitor in production

What you do not measure, you cannot fix. Log every request as structured data — input, output, latency, token usage, and a timestamp — so you can reproduce failures and trace cost back to specific calls.

```python
import json, time

start = time.perf_counter()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)
log = {
    "ts": time.time(),
    "latency_s": round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3),
    "input_tokens": msg.usage.input_tokens,
    "output_tokens": msg.usage.output_tokens,
}
print(json.dumps(log))
```

Feed these logs into a dashboard, set **alerts** when latency or error rate cross a threshold, and re-run your eval set on a sample of real traffic to catch **drift** early.

## Your task

Add request logging to one of your deployed features and write a 10-case eval set you can run with a single command.

slides.narration: Welcome back. You've built an A I feature and shipped it. But how do you know it actually works, and keeps working? In this lesson we'll cover two practices that answer exactly that: evaluating your system before you ship, and monitoring it once it's live. By the end you'll be able to measure quality, latency, and cost, and catch problems before your users do.

slides.title: Two questions
bullets: Evaluation: is it good enough to ship?
Monitoring: is it still good live?
You need both, not one.
Quality can rot silently over time.
slides.narration: There are really two separate questions here. Offline evaluation asks: is this good enough to release? It runs against a fixed test set before you deploy. Production monitoring asks: is it still good now that real users are hitting it? A system can pass every test at launch and quietly get worse as the world changes. So you need both.

slides.title: Build an eval set
bullets: A small set of inputs plus expected outputs.
Even 20 to 50 cases catch real bugs.
Run it automatically on every change.
slides.narration: An eval set is just a small collection of representative inputs paired with what you expect the system to produce. You don't need thousands; even twenty to fifty carefully chosen cases catch a surprising number of regressions. The key is to run them automatically, so every code change is checked before it goes out.

slides.title: Run the evals
bullets: Call the Claude Messages A P I.
Compare output to expected.
Count how many pass.
slides.code:
msg = client.messages.create(
  model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
  max_tokens=1024,
  messages=[{"role":"user",
             "content": question}],
)
text = msg.content[0].text
slides.narration: Running the evals is straightforward. For each case you call the Claude Messages A P I, take the model's reply, and check whether it matches what you expected. Then you count how many passed. Keep your A P I key in an environment variable, never in the code. If the pass rate drops after a change, you've caught a regression before your users did.

slides.title: Pick the right metrics
bullets: Accuracy or quality of the answer.
Latency: watch p95, not the average.
Cost: tokens in plus tokens out.
Error rate: failed or refused calls.
slides.narration: Different questions need different numbers, so track a handful. Accuracy or quality: did the answer meet the rubric? Latency: how fast was it, and crucially watch the ninety-fifth percentile, not just the average, because a slow tail can hide behind a healthy-looking mean. Cost: tokens in plus tokens out times the price. And error rate: how often did a call fail or get refused.

slides.title: LLM as a judge
bullets: Open answers have no single right string.
Exact match wrongly fails valid answers.
Ask a model to score against a rubric.
slides.code:
prompt = (
  f"Q: {question}\nA: {response}\n"
  "Score 1-5 for correctness. "
  "Reply with only the number."
)
slides.narration: For open-ended answers there's no single correct string, so exact matching fails: a perfectly good reply worded differently would be marked wrong. The fix is to use a model as a judge. You give a judge model the question, the answer, and a clear rubric, and ask it to score, say, one to five. Keep the rubric specific, and ask for just the number so it's easy to parse.

slides.title: Log everything
bullets: What you don't measure, you can't fix.
Log input, output, latency, tokens, time.
Structured logs let you reproduce bugs.
slides.narration: What you don't measure, you can't fix. So log every request as structured data: the input, the output, how long it took, the token usage, and a timestamp. The usage object on each response gives you the exact input and output token counts for free. With these logs you can reproduce a failure, trace a cost spike back to specific calls, and prove whether a change helped or hurt.

slides.title: Monitor and alert
bullets: Push logs into a dashboard.
Alert when latency or errors spike.
Re-run evals on real traffic samples.
slides.narration: Logs on their own aren't enough; you need to watch them. Feed them into a dashboard so trends are visible at a glance. Set alerts so that when latency or the error rate crosses a threshold, you get told immediately rather than hearing it from an angry user. And periodically re-run your eval set on a sample of real traffic to keep an eye on quality.

slides.title: Watch for drift
bullets: Inputs change even when code doesn't.
Quality can degrade silently.
Drift is why launch-day evals aren't enough.
slides.narration: Here's the subtle danger: drift. Your code might not change at all, but the real-world inputs do. Users ask new kinds of questions, the topics they care about shift, and slowly your system's quality degrades. That's exactly why passing evals on launch day isn't enough. Continuous monitoring and periodic re-evaluation are how you catch drift before it becomes a real problem.
